text:
Yes — but only in a limited, carefully controlled sense.

A person should have some right to be forgotten, even when the information is true, because punishment in a decent society is not supposed to last forever. If someone committed a serious offence twenty years ago, served the legal sentence, and has not reoffended, then the permanent, effortless visibility of that past can become a form of extra-judicial lifelong punishment. The internet changes the nature of memory: what once faded into obscurity through time now remains instantly searchable, globally accessible, and endlessly repeatable. That creates a strong moral case for allowing some past wrongdoing to recede from public view.

The strongest argument for such a right is rehabilitation. Most legal systems claim not only to punish but also to reform. That ideal is hollow if a person can never realistically escape their worst act. Stable employment, housing, relationships, and community trust are all harder to rebuild when an old conviction appears immediately in every search result. If we want people to become law-abiding citizens, we must leave room for them to do so. In the case of someone convicted of a serious offence twenty years ago who has lived responsibly ever since, continued algorithmic exposure may serve little public good while imposing enormous personal and social cost.

There is also a distinction between truth and present relevance. A true fact is not necessarily always deserving of equal public prominence forever. News reports are written for a moment. Twenty years later, the public interest may be much weaker, especially if the person is not a public official, not seeking a position of special trust, and poses no continuing danger. The issue is not falsifying history but recognizing that universal, permanent accessibility is different from archival existence. Information can remain in records and archives without being made maximally visible in ordinary public searches.

Still, the right cannot be absolute. Serious offences matter, and the public sometimes has a legitimate interest in knowing. If the person now works in a field connected to the past offence — for example, a convicted financial fraudster seeking control over clients’ money, or a violent offender applying to work with vulnerable people — concealment could put others at risk. Likewise, public figures, those in positions of power, or cases of major historical importance should face a much higher bar for removal. Victims’ interests matter too; a right to be forgotten must not become a right to erase the reality of harm done.

So the best position is a qualified one: not deletion of history, but reduction of unnecessary exposure. Search engines might de-index old reports from name-based searches after a long crime-free period. Archives could remain intact. Courts or independent regulators could weigh factors such as the seriousness of the offence, time elapsed, evidence of rehabilitation, current public role, and ongoing risk. This approach respects both public memory and the possibility of redemption.

In the specific case of a person convicted of a serious offence twenty years ago who has not reoffended, I would argue that they should generally have a right to limit easy public access to that information, unless there is a clear present public interest in keeping it prominent. A humane society should remember that people are more than the worst thing they have done. Without some possibility of being forgotten, forgiveness becomes merely rhetorical.
